n: A hard verse. The KJV reads it as praise for one who withdraws to seek wisdom. Many modern translations read it the other way: a person who isolates himself pursues his own desires and rejects sound judgment.

f.g: The Hebrew is debated: either withdrawing to study, or selfishly cutting himself off from others.
intermeddleth = engages with, or quarrels against.

n: A fool doesn’t care to understand; he only wants to air his own opinions.

f.w: that his heart may discover itself
f.g: discover = reveal, uncover—to show off his own views.

n: Wickedness brings contempt with it, and shameful behavior brings disgrace.
A person’s words can run deep like waters; the source of wisdom flows like a fresh, bubbling brook.
It is wrong to show favor to the guilty or to deny justice to the innocent.

f.w: accept the person of the wicked
f.g: Show partiality—literally “lift up the face” of the wicked.

n: A fool’s words start fights, and his mouth practically invites a beating.
A fool’s own mouth ruins him; his words become a trap for his life.
Gossip is like tasty bites of food that people swallow eagerly—and it sinks deep inside. The image is about how easily rumors are absorbed.

f.g: Hebrew likely means “delicious morsels”—gossip is tempting to swallow.

n: Laziness is a close relative of destruction. Neglect destroys as surely as wastefulness.

f.g: A destroyer; one who ruins things.

n: The Lord’s name—his character and presence—is a tall fortress where the righteous run and find safety.

f.w: The name of the LORD is a strong tower

n: The rich imagine their wealth is a fortress and a high wall around them—but it’s only in their imagination. Compare verse 10.
Pride comes right before destruction, and humility comes before honor.
Answering before you’ve heard the whole story is foolish and embarrassing. Listen first.

f.w: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it

n: A person’s spirit can carry them through physical illness, but who can endure a crushed spirit? Emotional wounds are among the heaviest.

f.w: a wounded spirit who can bear?

n: Discerning hearts acquire knowledge, and wise ears go looking for it.
A gift opens doors and gains access to important people. This observes how influence works; it can be used well or badly.
The first to tell his side in a dispute sounds right—until someone else cross-examines him. Hear both sides.
Casting lots settled disputes and kept powerful rivals from fighting.

f.g: Lots were cast to decide matters, trusting God to direct the result.

n: A wounded brother is harder to win back than a fortified city; family quarrels are like locked castle gates.

f.g: Heavy bolts on a fortress gate.

n: Your words are like crops: you’ll eat the harvest of what you say.
The tongue holds the power of life and death; those who love to talk will eat the results.

f.w: Death and life are in the power of the tongue

n: Finding a wife is finding something good, a sign of the Lord’s favor. Marriage is seen as a blessing from God.

f.w: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing

n: The poor must plead for mercy, while the rich answer harshly. An honest observation about how wealth can change people.

The KJV says to have friends, be friendly. Many translators read: a person of many companions may come to ruin, but a true friend sticks closer than a brother. Christians often see the Savior as that truest friend.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean “may come to ruin”—too many shallow friends can harm you.

f.w: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother
